AgreeLab: AgreeLab help 1/9: Agreement beyond chance
Two raters sort the same N items into k
categories.  Observed agreement po = the
share on the diagonal of the table.
Some agreement happens by chance: if the
raters chose independently at their own
rates, pe = sum of (row share × column share).
Cohen's kappa (1960) = (po - pe)/(1 - pe):
the share of the possible agreement beyond
chance that was reached.  1 = perfect,
0 = chance level, below 0 = worse than chance.
Tiles page: drag a count from an off-diagonal
tile to a diagonal one and watch kappa rise.

AgreeLab help 2/9: SE, CI and the test
Two different SEs (Fleiss, Cohen & Everitt 1969, Psychol Bull
- the large-sample SE gives the 95% CI, kappa ± 1.96 SE (rough
when N is small);
- SE₀, the SE if kappa were 0, gives the test: z = kappa/SE₀,
one-sided p.
p = P(a kappa this big | H₀: kappa = 0).
It is not the chance that H₀ is true, and 'better than chance' is
easy to reach: raters who agree on only 1 item in 3 can reach it.
The CI says how much agreement there is, and how precisely it
is known.

AgreeLab help 3/9: Kappa max and the paradox
kappa max (Cohen 1960): with these row and
column totals, at most sum of min(row, col)
can agree.  Raters who use the categories at
different rates can never reach kappa = 1.
The paradox (Feinstein & Cicchetti 1990):
high po, low kappa, when one category is
very common: pe is then high too.  Load the
two paradox tables (illustrative numbers):
both have po = 0.85; kappa 0.32 and 0.70.
PABAK = (k po - 1)/(k - 1) (Byrt, Bishop &
Carlin 1993) removes prevalence and bias:
it is po rescaled.  Report po, the margins
and kappa together, not kappa alone.

AgreeLab help 4/9: Weighted kappa
Ordered categories (certain, probable, ...):
a near miss is better than a far one.
Weighted kappa (Cohen 1968) gives tile i, j
the credit w(i, j), 1 on the diagonal:
linear 1 - |i - j|/(k - 1)
(Cicchetti & Allison 1971);
quadratic 1 - (i - j)²/(k - 1)²
(Fleiss & Cohen 1973).
Then po and pe use the weights, and
kappa_w = (po_w - pe_w)/(1 - pe_w); SEs as
for kappa (Fleiss, Cohen & Everitt 1969).
Quadratic weights give the most credit to
near misses.  Choose weights before the data.

AgreeLab help 5/9: Many raters, Fleiss' kappa
Each of N subjects gets m ratings (Fleiss
1971); the raters may differ by subject.
Data: counts n(i, j) = how many put subject i
in category j (each row adds to m).
P_i = share of subject i's m(m-1)/2 rater
pairs that agree; P = their mean.
Pe = sum of p_j², p_j = category j's share.
kappa = (P - Pe)/(1 - Pe); per category too.
SE under H₀ only (Fleiss, Nee & Landis 1979,
Psychol Bull 86:974): a test, but no CI.

AgreeLab help 9/9: Agreement and forensic work
Agreement is reliability, not accuracy:
two examiners can agree and both be wrong.
Accuracy needs cases where the truth is
known (ground truth), not a second opinion.
Kappa depends on the mix of cases (the
paradox), so two studies' kappas compare
only if their case mixes are alike.
Kappa assumes independent ratings: a
verifier who knows the first conclusion is
not an independent rater.
A teaching aid only: not validated for
forensic, clinical or legal use.

AnovaLab: AnovaLab help 1/10: What one-way ANOVA asks
H₀: every group has the same population mean μ.
ANOVA splits the total spread (SS) in two:
between: n × (group mean - grand mean)²
within: (value - its own group mean)²
MS = SS / df;  F = MS between / MS within.
If H₀ is true, F is near 1 and follows the F-curve
with (k - 1) and (N - k) df; p = P(F this big | H₀).
A small p is evidence that SOME mean differs:
not which (Pairs page), not how much (eta²).
eta² = SS between / SS total; omega² (Hays)
subtracts the part chance alone would give.
Every value counts: 0 and negatives are data.

AnovaLab help 2/10: Welch and the checks
The F-test assumes equal spreads (and roughly normal groups).
Welch's F (1951) drops equal spreads: each group is weighted
by n / s².
Levene's test (Brown-Forsythe form) runs the one-way F on
|value - group median|; non-normal data affect it little.
Bartlett's χ² compares the s² directly: it is misled by
non-normal data.
In the insect-spray preset, s runs from 1.7 to 6.2 and Levene's
test flags it; compare the ordinary F with Welch's.
A check that is not significant is not proof of equal spreads: with
small groups the checks often miss real differences.

AnovaLab help 5/10: Dunnett's test
Dunnett's test compares every group with ONE control
group (a placebo, the usual method): (k - 1) comparisons,
not all the pairs.  With fewer comparisons, it finds a
real difference more often than Tukey's test does.
t = (group mean - control mean)/SE, SE from MS within
and both n.  A group differs when |t| > d crit, and d crit
keeps the chance of ANY false alarm in the family at α.
Adjusted p: the chance that the LARGEST |t| of the
family is this big when no group differs from the control.
Enter > Dunnett: pick the control.  It asks before it runs
(slow on a G1).  Two pages: the table, then the CIs drawn.
Two-sided; unequal n allowed.  Choose the control before
you see the data.  Dunnett (1955); p within 0.05 %.

CICatcher: CICatcher help 1/7: 95 % of WHAT?
Each line is the interval from ONE sample.
The green line is the truth (μ or p): the method never sees it. A
blue line caught it (the interval contains it); a red line missed it.
The 95 % is the share of intervals the METHOD catches in the
long run, not a property of any one interval. Keep adding
samples: the 'all' rate at the top of the screen settles near the
confidence level.
Any one interval either caught μ or missed it.
So say 'we are 95 % confident' -- meaning the method catches
the truth 95 % of the time -- not 'a 95 % chance μ is in
THIS interval'.

CICatcher help 3/7: Wald and Wilson
Wald:  ± z × √((1 - )/n), the textbook interval. Center and
width both come from , which fails when n × p is small:
at p = 0.10, n = 20 Wald catches only 87.6 % (exact binomial; it
claims 95 %).
12.2 % of those samples have  = 0: the Wald interval has ZERO
width and must miss.
Wilson (score) takes its SE from each possible p, not from ,
and keeps every p within z SEs of : never zero width, center
pulled toward 1/2. Same p and n: 95.7 %.
Wald needs n × p and n × (1 - p) to be 10 or more; at p = 0.10,
n = 100 it reaches 93.2 %.
Gray on the axis: impossible values (below 0, above 1). Only
Wald lines can reach them.

CICatcher help 4/7: Exact intervals
Exact (Clopper-Pearson) uses no normal curve:
it keeps every p for which your count is not in either α/2 tail of
Binomial(n, p).
A count has only n + 1 possible values, so no interval can catch
exactly 95 % at every p.
Exact makes sure it is NEVER LESS: at n = 20 its worst case over
every p is 95.8 %.
At p = 0.10, n = 20 it catches 98.9 % (Wilson 95.7 %, Wald 87.6
%); at 80 % or 90 % it still catches 95.7 %. The cost: longer lines
(wider intervals).
0 yeses: from 0 to 1 - (α/2)^(1/n), 0.168 at n = 20 and 95 %.

CICatcher help 5/7: Tolerance intervals
A confidence interval is about a mean.  A tolerance interval is
about single values:  ± k s is made to hold at least 90 % (or
95 %, or 99 %) of the whole population.
The green band is the middle 90 % of the population.  A blue
line holds at least 90 % of the population; a red line holds less.
Tap a line: the panel says how much of the population it holds.
The level is the share of samples whose line holds its 90 %:
the 'all' rate at the top settles near it.
k is larger than z = 1.645 because  and s are estimates: at
n = 10 and 95 %, k = 2.856.  k is worked out exactly here;
printed tables often give an approximation that differs in the
third digit.

ExhibitLab: ExhibitLab help 1/8: What the claim means
'At least 90% are drug, at 95% confidence':
if fewer than 90% of the N units held drug, a random sample of
this size would show this few negatives (or fewer) at most 5% of
the time: the METHOD rarely supports a false claim.  It does NOT
mean: a 95% probability that 90% are drug (a Bayesian
statement, page 2); that the untested units were analyzed; that a
given unit is drug;
anything about weight or purity.
'90%' of 100 units means at least 90 units.

ExhibitLab help 2/8: Frequentist or Bayesian?
Hypergeometric (frequentist): a statement about the PROCEDURE.
Suppose the claim is false by the smallest margin (K₀ drug
units); if what you found would then be rare (P ≤ 1 - c), it is
supported.  Bayesian (Aitken 1999; ENFSI 2009): about THIS
SEIZURE: P(at least p₀N are drug | what you found).  It needs a
prior : uniform Beta(1, 1) treats every proportion as equally
likely; Jeffreys Beta(0.5, 0.5) gives more weight to proportions
near 0 and 1.  The prior matters most when n is small.  Say
which one you used.

the smallest n is 8 at N = 10, 23 at N = 100, never
more than 29 however big N is (computed now; see Tables).

FitCheck help 3/12: Small counts and Merge
The χ² curve gives a trustworthy p only when
the E are not too small: every E ≥ 5, or
Cochran's rule (at most 20% of the E below 5

FitCheck help 7/12: Outliers: Dixon's test
DIXON'S OUTLIER TEST (the Outlier key; 3 to 30
values).  Is the lowest or the highest value
too far from the rest to come from the same
normal population?  Sort the values: x(1) is
the lowest, x(n) the highest.  The ratio is a
gap over a range: how far the value stands
from its neighbor, as a share of the spread.
0 = no gap; 1 = it stands alone.
The page draws every value as a dot, the
tested one in red, with its gap (red) and its
range (blue) above the dots.  It tests the end
with the bigger ratio.

FitCheck help 8/12: Outliers: which ratio
The ratio changes with n (Dixon 1953).  First
digit: the gap ends at the nearest value (1)
or the second-nearest (2).  Second digit: how
many values the range leaves off its far end.
3 to 7 values: r₁₀.  The gap to the nearest
value, over the whole range.
8 to 10: r₁₁.  The range leaves off 1 value.
11 to 13: r₂₁.  The gap to the second-nearest
value; the range leaves off 1.
14 to 30: r₂₂.  The range leaves off 2 values.
Why: a second outlier, beside the first or at
the far end, would hide the first.  The later
ratios guard against that.

FitCheck help 9/12: Outliers: the p and its limits
THE P is the chance, in a normal sample of
this size, of a ratio this big or bigger at
that end.  FitCheck computes it; a printed
table of critical values can differ from it in
the third decimal (McBane 2006).
The test takes the end with the bigger ratio,
so the p it reports is for either end: twice
the one-end p, as in the printed tables.  That
is an upper limit.
A small p is a reason to check the value: was
it misread, mistyped, or from another
population?  It is no license to delete it.
The p assumes normal data (see the Q-Q plot).
Values tied by rounding can make the ratio 1.

RankLab help 3/10: Sign test, signed-rank
Both test H₀: the median of d is 0.  Zeros
are dropped: n counts the nonzero d only.
SIGN: S+ = number of d > 0, Binomial(n, 1/2)
under H₀; exact p from BINOMIAL_CDF; two-
sided = 2 × the smaller tail (at most 1).
SIGNED-RANK: rank |d| (midranks); T+ = the
sum of the ranks of d > 0.  Under H₀ each
sign is + or - with chance 1/2, 2^n patterns;
RankLab counts them all (ties too), n ≤ 50.
Effect r = (T+ - T-)/(n(n+1)/2).  Estimate:
Hodges-Lehmann = the median of all Walsh
averages (d_i + d_j)/2, i ≤ j (n ≤ 100).

MANN-WHITNEY: rank both groups together;
U₁ = R₁ - n₁(n₁ + 1)/2 = the (X, Y) pairs with

RankLab help 7/10: The runs test
THE RUNS TEST asks whether the ORDER of a sequence is
random.  It is not a rank test: it only counts.  A RUN is a
stretch of the same kind:  R R R R B R R R  has 3 runs.
Two kinds (red or black, pass or fail) are used as they are.
Numbers are cut at their median into above and below; a value
equal to the median is dropped.
TOO FEW runs: like values cluster (a drift, a trend, streaks).
TOO MANY runs: the two kinds alternate more than chance does.
Tails: lower = too few, upper = too many, two-sided = either.
EXACT p: every order of the two kinds is equally likely under
H₀; RankLab counts the orders (n ≤ 2,000).
NORMAL: z = (runs - mean)/SD, mean = 2 n₁ n₂/n + 1.
Plot: a square for each value; numbers also as a chart (More).

ResampLab: ResampLab help 1/5: Shuffling labels
A permutation test asks: if the group labels
did not matter (H₀), how often would chance
alone give a difference as big as the one we
saw?
Once: the pooled values are shuffled into new
groups of the same sizes, and the new
difference d is added to the histogram.  Red
line: the observed d; red dots: shuffles at
least as extreme.
p = (as extreme)/(shuffles).  Small p: the
labels seem to matter.  Large p: no evidence
that they do (not proof that they don't).
Assumes: under H₀ the labels could be swapped
without changing anything, which is true when
the groups were made by random assignment.

ResampLab help 3/5: The bootstrap
Treat the sample as the population: draw n
values WITH replacement (a stack of dots = a
value picked more than once) and compute the
statistic.  Repeat B times: their spread
estimates its SE.
Percentile: the middle 95% of the B values.

estimate.  BCa: corrected for bias (z₀) and
skew (a); use B ≥ 1,000.  t:  ± t s/√n, to
compare.

percentile, and Welch's t for means.
With small samples the intervals are too
narrow: use n of about 15 or more.

ScatterLab help 2/7: r², the share explained
All variation in y: SST = sum (y - ȳ)², the squared distances of
the points from the flat line at ȳ.
What the line leaves: SSE = sum (y - ŷ)².

accounts for.  r² = 0.64 means 64% explained and 36% left over
in the residuals.  (It is also r times r.)
Try it: Guess starts flat, at ȳ, so 'your SSE' starts at SST.  The best
line brings it down to SSE; the drop, as a share of SST, is r².

StudRange help 3/5: Why q and not t
Two means (k = 2): q = t·√2 exactly, so
q crit = √2 · t crit (two-sided).
k means make k(k−1)/2 pairs. A t-test on each
at α finds SOME difference far more often
than α: that is the family-wise error rate. q
uses the range (the largest mean minus the
smallest), so q > q crit has chance α for the
whole family of pairs.

TDist3D: TDist3D help 1/4: What the surface is
When σ is unknown, s takes its place in t = ( − μ) / (s/√n), and
s is a different number in every sample: t varies more than z
does, and the extra variation goes into the tails.
Student's t has one parameter: degrees of freedom, ν = (n − 1).
This surface puts the curves one behind another: t runs across,
ν runs away from you, 0.5 at the front to 10 at the back; the
height is the density f(t; ν).
Every curve has area 1.  The front curves (small ν) are low in the
middle and high in the tails; the back curves come close to
N(0,1), the normal curve, drawn as gray dots beyond the back
edge (ν = ∞).

TrendTest: TrendTest help 1/3: χ² for trend, the idea
Exposure levels have an ORDER (dose, hours, grade).  Pearson's
χ², (k-1) df, asks only 'do the proportions differ?'.  The trend test
(1 df) asks 'do they rise or fall steadily with the score?'
With 1 df the trend test puts all its evidence into one question,
so it has more power than Pearson's when the proportions
really do lie near a straight line.
Pearson's χ² minus the trend χ², (k-2) df, measures how far the
proportions are from a straight line; a large value means they do
not follow one.
Scores: use the doses themselves when known;
otherwise 1, 2, 3 ...  The trend test's answer depends on how the
scores are spaced; Pearson's does not.  The Scores key switches
among 1, 2, 3 ..., the scores as entered, and midranks.
